A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same brain-to-text data-leakage study and splitting criterion. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding algorithms, experiments, figures, and tables can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v3 reports original leakage measurements, encoder-loss curves, training-setting analyses, and decoding benchmarks on Narratives and ZuCo in Tables 1–4 and Figure 4.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations on an additional test set, shuffled-input experiments, and decoding without teacher forcing in Tables 3, 4, and 6.

M1.justification: The EEG subject–text and fMRI subject–story splitting procedures remain, and Algorithms 1–2 are identical. The expanded graph formulation and revised step numbering document the existing procedure; they do not establish a changed algorithm or decoding model.

E1.justification: v4 extends testing to randomly shuffled, noise-like brain-signal inputs. Narratives/fMRI and ZuCo/EEG remain the datasets and decoding tasks; the additional leakage-free test partition stays within this coverage.

E2.justification: The five existing splitting comparators and the UniCoRN and EEG2Text models are retained. The randomly initialized UniCoRN variant also remains in the training analysis. Newly cited work is not introduced as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: v4 adds substantial evaluation protocols: a separate leakage-free test partition, shuffled-input controls, and generation without teacher forcing. Existing split ratios and documented training budgets remain. Its fMRI concatenation endpoint changes from j+L−1 to j+L while the appendix retains L=10, leaving an actual window-length change unresolved.

E4.justification: New analyses test generalization to leakage-free data, dependence on brain-signal input, and whether leakage effects persist without teacher forcing. The earlier encoder-loss and epoch/learning-rate analyses remain; v3 Tables 2–3 move to v4 Appendix E as Tables 7–8.

E5.justification: v4 Table 2 introduces mean-plus/minus summaries for leakage rates, replacing v3 Table 1's individual seed columns and averages. Both versions specify four runs with seeds 1–4, so no increased run count is established. The meaning of the plus/minus quantity is not explicitly defined.

E6.justification: Tables 3, 4, and 6 add substantial condition-specific decoding results. ZuCo method (d)'s TSLR changes from 0.00% to 12.88±0.04%. The fair-benchmark values remain unchanged between v3 Table 4 and v4 Table 5. Retained training tables swap ROUGE R/F headers without rearranging values, creating metric-label ambiguities.

T1.justification: v4 adds directed four-partite multigraph definitions, formal leakage definitions, and explicit graph-based splitting equations. New Appendix D supplies arguments for criterion equivalence, zero leakage, and the necessity of discarding samples, substantially extending v3's set rules and graph description.

C1.justification: The central leakage diagnosis, leakage-free splitting, and rebenchmarking contributions remain. The priority claim changes from proposing the first cross-subject splitting criterion to first identifying leakage in existing splitting methods. The conclusion explicitly clarifies that improving decoding architectures is outside the paper's scope.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations of shuffled-input and teacher-forcing controls, argues that discarding samples is unavoidable, and explicitly identifies ECoG/MEG evaluation as future work. The main memorization explanation remains. Appendix E still describes EEG method (d) as free of text leakage, conflicting with the revised main-text findings.

D1.justification: v4 adds architectural descriptions of the evaluated models in Section 3.3 but removes v3's NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB hardware disclosure. The implementation appendix otherwise retains the filtering references, hyperparameters, batch sizes, training schedules, and sample-length setting.

R1.justification: v4 adds Allen, Chang, Hasson, Pereira, and Jo references for dataset context, shared brain responses, and teacher-forcing concerns, while removing Ye et al. The existing related-work discussion survives in Appendix A, and the novelty claim is modestly repositioned toward identifying leakage.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, Section 2 becomes graph-oriented preliminaries, and related work moves to Appendix A. Methodology and experimental discussion are reorganized, training analyses move to Appendix E, and the conclusion gains discussion. The title, author list, and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 becomes a staged graph-construction illustration, a model/leakage diagram is added, and splitting diagrams are redrawn. v4 adds a leakage-summary table and three colored diagnostic tables, restructures the leakage-rate table, reduces the benchmark table's display size, and relocates the retained training tables.

improvement.justification: The additional leakage-free tests, shuffled-input controls, and decoding without teacher forcing provide more direct support for the leakage argument than v3's loss and training-duration analyses. These gains are limited by unreconciled EEG method (d) findings, conflicting ROUGE labels, and Appendix D's discard-necessity argument assuming cross-story subject overlap without establishing it generally.
